P1.evidence: No setter suffix and no application referenced, so P1a does not apply. The frame ran in its usual three-part form with the disqualification clause: 'go into what you're trying to achieve, see if we can help you with that, where you're currently at. If we can help you bridge that gap, I'll take it to how I feel like we can fit in there. If not, perfectly fine. I'll point you in the right direction. Okay?' — agreement was sought and given. The open question is a clear miss: after the frame the call went into several minutes of camera and audio troubleshooting, and the prospect simply began talking about himself. 'What are you potentially looking for help with?' was never asked, and the agenda for the first ten minutes was set entirely by the prospect's own opening monologue.

P2.evidence: Sharply uneven. The injury inventory is the best-executed baseline work in the batch: the rep asked deliberately and with the right reason — 'just to make sure I actually know them all right, because it is important for us that we don't make things worse. It's the forearms a little bit, shoulders, rear delts, anything else?' — enumerated all five sites, ran a 1-to-10 frequency scale, established they are activation-dependent rather than constant, and asked how long ('months, years'). Current training, results and diet were all properly probed, including the genuinely useful finding that two swims and an hour of yoga a week transform his blood sugar. Against that: not one of age, height or weight was asked — age and weight were volunteered and height was never obtained at all. Health conditions were never asked, so the diabetes arrived unprompted and was never followed up for medication, control or clinical oversight. Sleep was never mentioned. Energy was never asked, and when the prospect volunteered 'my energy levels are a little bit weak' the rep did not pick it up, which matters for a fasting diabetic about to start strenuous training.

P3.evidence: The mechanics ran well. The priority question was asked cleanly — 'what is the main thing that you want to focus on that you feel like, okay, this actually needs to change the quickest?' — and produced 'movement without pain'. The can't-do question landed golf, the motorcycle and testing himself with weight. The bridge ran close to verbatim: 'everything that we've talked about is basically around physical, but a lot of times it's driven by a why in the more so personal aspect. So what would that do to you personally?' Two accurate reflect-backs ran with confirmation checks. Scored partial rather than hit because the deepest layer never arrived: 'who else does that impact?' was never asked, and no partner, children or family were mentioned once in fifty-five minutes. The why stopped at the prospect's own trajectory and mental health. The manager reviewing this call reached the same conclusion independently — 'I think we missed a deep goal section' — and noted the prospect was never sold on an identity or an image of his changed life.

P4.evidence: The strongest phase in the batch and the best sequence the rep ran all week. History was covered — prior PT trial sessions, and what he has done about it in the intervening years ('Not very much'). The blocker question then produced something genuinely valuable. The prospect said he wanted 'someone who doesn't have the same resistance that I might have'; the rep pushed with 'As in? Any resistance, like for example, laziness, excuses. Would you say that you make excuses?' and got the prospect to name and connect his own two obstacles unprompted: 'to not do anything based on injuries is an excuse' and 'the laziness loves the injuries. So I can't have that. And that needs to link between laziness and injuries. It just needs to cut.' That is exactly what P4e is for. Marked down because the reason the previous PT lapsed was asked but returned nothing, and rather than sitting with the silence the rep supplied the answer himself — 'it sounds like the things that you're mainly looking for are the guidance, accountability' — leading the witness. The 'why can't you stick to it on your own?' challenge only surfaced later, as an objection response.

P5.evidence: Substantively run. The rep set up the negative projection with the rationale attached — 'when we see what the bad direction is, it's so much easier to stay away from it because we always run faster from a line than we run towards something' — and got a concrete answer: the injuries persist and worsen, golf is already gone, the motorcycle grip was becoming painful. The settle question ran, though phrased as a statement he agreed with rather than an open question, and produced the strongest emotional material in the call: 'there's massive emotional, mental health, emotional health changes that come from getting stronger'. The dentistry analogy about patients who are told to brush better and do not until they decide for themselves was well chosen and landed. But 'why not?' was never asked cleanly, and the line-in-the-sand question was never put at all, which left the frame vivid but without a commitment moment attached to it.

P6.evidence: The belief checks ran repeatedly and well — after the training pillar, after nutrition, and finally 'outside of the pricing, do you feel like this is something I see myself starting with?' The isolation attempt was there in substance too, and the rep even probed the hedge: told 'Yeah, potentially', he asked 'What's making you say potentially?' and 'is there something that springs out for you?' P6c is nonetheless a clear miss and the pivotal error of the call. The script says to move forward only on a clear yes and to return to Phase 5 if hesitation surfaces. The rep received 'Yeah, potentially', then 'I haven't made a decision yet, so... potentially, yes', identified the problem out loud himself — 'that potentially just sounds unsure, right? So it's good that you mentioned that' — and went straight to price anyway. He also carried two unresolved blockers into the close: the forearm safety concern and an unmet request for a client reference.

P11.evidence: Price was presented and a close was attempted, but the prospect declined outright and none of the payment or onboarding steps became reachable. Scored not applicable so a clean loss is not penalised for steps that only exist after agreement.

objection_plays.detail: The best-run money play in the batch on the isolation half, and correctly abandoned on the other. Isolation ran twice — 'outside of the money, does it sound like you see yourself going through it, it's just the money aspect. Is that true?' — and the HOW-versus-SHOULD reframe ran almost verbatim: 'Is it more of a, should I do this, or is it more of a, how should I do this for you?', answered 'It's should I do this.' The break-it-up option was offered. None of the six financial-picture questions ran, which was the right judgement rather than an omission: the prospect had just confirmed this was a belief problem, not a capacity one, so financing was not the lever. The genuine failure is what followed. Having correctly diagnosed a 'should I' problem, the script's own logic points back to Phase 5 and the value case. The rep asked one open question, accepted the answer and closed the call.

Triggered early and hard — 'if this is how it is, I ain't going to do it. I'm just going to make things worse' — and again at the commitment check, where the prospect said his yes depended on 'a few days of doing it, not getting the forearm injuries'. This is fear of harm, the exact territory OE covers. Two proof-shaped moves ran: Trevor having started with kettlebells because of his own injuries, and the rep's father taking up kettlebells at 48 with a hernia. Neither is scripted, and the actual play did not run — no 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', no pain-versus-pleasure question, no bridge, no plane analogy, no 'how will you know if you never actually try?'. The fear was never named as fear and was answered with technical reassurance instead.

Script gap, and the second appearance of the gap already logged in the playbook from the Tyron Giuliani call. The prospect presented with five active injury sites, diabetes, an abandoned deadlift and squat history, and pain performing the programme's core movement during a trial he had run specifically to test it. There is no scripted path for a clinical fit objection, no screening step and no clearance requirement, so the rep improvised a reassurance that the pain was a form problem which would disappear. Whether the programme can actually serve this body is unresolved and unresolvable within the current script.

Script gap. The prospect asked for something reasonable and specific — an independent, UK-based current client he could speak to about the experience of working with Trevor, explicitly not about outcomes. The rep had nothing: 'I've got no idea, to be honest. No idea.' There is no reference process, no client list and no play for a social-proof request, so the rep substituted online testimonials and his own history as a client, neither of which is independent. The prospect restated the request unmet and the call moved on. Worth escalating as a missing sales asset rather than a rep failure.

notes: The best discovery of the batch on injuries and root cause — the enumeration of five injury sites and the extraction of 'the laziness loves the injuries' are both textbook. It was undone at the commitment check, where the rep heard 'potentially', said out loud that it sounded unsure, and went to price anyway carrying two live blockers: an unresolved fear that the movements would worsen his injuries, and an unmet request for a client reference. Coach on stopping at 'potentially' and returning to Phase 5, and on treating a safety objection as the fear play rather than as a technical question. Separately, this call needed a clinical stop that the process does not contain.
